replacement: People have always noticed that the habits of legal business do not prepare men to exercise administrative authority. The Americans took from the English, their forefathers, an institution that the continent of Europe does not know: the Justices of the Peace. The Justice of the Peace stands halfway between the magistrate and the ordinary man of the world, between the civil officer and the judge. He is a well-informed citizen, though not necessarily someone trained in the law. His office simply requires him to enforce the police regulations of society, and for that task good sense and integrity count for more than legal science. The justice brings to the administration a certain taste for established forms and for publicity, which makes him a most unserviceable instrument of despotism. At the same time, he is free of the superstitions that make legal officers poor members of a government. The Americans have adopted the English system of justices of the peace, but they have removed the aristocratic character it has in the mother country. The Governor of Massachusetts *p appoints a certain number of justices of the peace in every county, for terms of seven years. *q He also chooses three of them from the whole body of justices, and in each county these three form what is called the Court of Sessions. The justices take a personal share in public business. Sometimes they receive administrative functions alongside elected officers, *r and sometimes they form a tribunal before which the magistrates summarily prosecute a refractory citizen, or the citizens report abuses by a magistrate. But the Court of Sessions is where they exercise their most important functions. This court meets twice a year in the county town, and in Massachusetts it has the power to enforce the obedience of most *s public officers. *t It should be noted that in Massachusetts the Court of Sessions is at once an administrative body in the proper sense and a political tribunal. Some have claimed that the county is a purely administrative division. The Court of Sessions handles the few affairs that concern several townships, or all the townships of the county in common, and that therefore cannot be left to any one of them. *u In everything that concerns county business, its duties are purely administrative. If in its investigations it sometimes borrows the forms of judicial procedure, it does so only to inform itself, *v or as a guarantee to the community it presides over. But when the administration of a township is brought before it, it always acts as a judicial body, and in a few cases as an official assembly.
